title: Deques, and Building One Structure from Another
quickIdea: A deque allows insertion and deletion at both ends. A queue can be built from two stacks with O(1) amortised operations, and the amortisation is what GATE tests.
remember: Deque variants: input-restricted allows insertion at one end only and deletion at both; output-restricted allows deletion at one end only and insertion at both. A deque can act as a stack (use one end) or as a queue (insert one end, delete the other).

Queue from two stacks, amortised-O(1) method: enqueue always pushes onto stack in; dequeue pops from stack out, first moving every element of in to out when out is empty. Each element moves at most once, so the total work over n operations is O(n).
Worst-case single dequeue in that method is O(k) for a queue holding k elements - the amortised bound does not make any one call constant.
Stack from two queues: push enqueues into q1, pop moves all but the last element of q1 into q2, returns the last, then swaps the queues. Push is O(1) and pop is O(n).
Priority queue is a different structure: it returns the smallest or largest key, not the oldest element, and it is covered with binary heaps rather than with queues.

example.prompt: GATE CSE 2006 Q.49. A queue is built from stacks S1 and S2: insert pushes onto S1; delete moves all of S1 to S2 when S2 is empty, then pops S2. With n inserts and m <= n deletes in any order, bound the number of push operations x and pop operations y.
example.work: Best case, alternating: each delete moves one element across, so pushes are n (inserts) plus m (the moves) = n + m, and pops are 2m (one move out of S1 and one out of S2 per delete). Worst case, all inserts first: the first delete moves all n elements, so pushes are n + n = 2n and pops are n moves plus m returns = n + m. The paper writes the push bound as n + m <= x < 2n; the all-inserts-first order reaches x = 2n exactly, so the bound is read as x <= 2n, and no other option fits either way.
example.answer: Option (A) of the paper: n + m <= x < 2n and 2m <= y <= n + m (with x = 2n attained in the all-inserts-first order).

gateAngle: Amortised cost questions are answered by counting the total work over the whole sequence rather than the worst single call. State the total first, then read the bound off it - that ordering avoids the usual mistake of quoting O(1) for a dequeue that just moved k elements. Note the one loose end in this question: the paper's strict upper bound x < 2n is reached exactly when every insert precedes every delete, so treat it as x <= 2n and check the options against that.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Using the two-stack queue, insert 1, 2, 3 then delete once, then insert 4, then delete twice. List the deleted values and give the total number of stack pushes and pops.
variations.answer: Deletions 1, 2, 3; total pushes 7 and total pops 6.
variations.why: Inserts 1, 2, 3 push onto S1 (3 pushes). The first delete moves 3 elements to S2 (3 pops, 3 pushes) and pops 1 (1 pop). Insert 4 is one push. The next two deletes pop 2 then 3, one pop each. Pushes 3 + 3 + 1 = 7; pops 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6 - the same counting that produces the 2006 bounds.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: An input-restricted deque allows insertion at one end only. Can it still simulate a stack?
variations.why: A stack needs insertion and deletion at the same end, and an input-restricted deque permits deletion at both ends, so choose that end for both operations. Restricting the input end does not restrict the output end.

trap.what: Reporting O(1) as the worst-case cost of a dequeue in the two-stack queue.
trap.why: The amortised bound is a total-over-the-sequence statement. A single dequeue that finds the out stack empty must move every queued element, which is O(k) for that call.
trap.counterexample: Insert 1,000 elements and then delete one. That single dequeue performs 1,000 pops and 1,000 pushes before returning the first element - clearly not O(1), though 1,000 alternating operations are O(1) each on average.

check.question: In the two-stack queue holding k elements, what is the worst-case cost of one dequeue, and what is the amortised cost?
check.explanation: When the out stack is empty the whole in stack must be reversed, which is k moves. Each element is moved at most once over its lifetime, so the total for n operations is O(n) and the amortised cost per operation is constant.
